shortQuestions: Many historical monuments are made of marble or limestone (calcium carbonate). Acids in acid rain react with it: CaCO₃ + H₂SO₄ → CaSO₄ + H₂O + CO₂.
The stone slowly dissolves and crumbles ('stone cancer'), surfaces become pitted and discoloured, carvings lose their detail (e.g. the Taj Mahal), and metal parts corrode. This damage is permanent.
(a) Contaminant: a substance that is not normally present in the environment (or is present in larger than natural amounts); it may or may not be harmful.
(b) Pollutant: a contaminant present in amounts that cause harmful effects to living organisms, materials or the environment.
(c) Acid rain: rain (or snow, fog) with pH less than 5.6, caused by dissolved oxides of sulphur and nitrogen forming H₂SO₄ and HNO₃.

(d) Biochemical oxygen demand (BOD): the amount of dissolved oxygen (mg L⁻¹) needed by micro-organisms to decompose the organic matter in a water sample over 5 days at 20 °C; a high BOD indicates heavy organic pollution.
(e) Smog: a mixture of smoke and fog — polluted air; classical smog contains SO₂, soot and fog, while photochemical smog contains NOₓ, hydrocarbons, O₃ and PAN formed in sunlight.
Dissolved oxygen is essential for fish and other aquatic animals and plants to respire (most fish need more than about 5 ppm).

It allows aerobic bacteria to decompose organic matter, so water purifies itself. Clean water has about 8–10 ppm DO; low DO shows organic pollution and leads to bad smells and the death of aquatic life.
Use low-sulphur fuels (or remove sulphur from fuels and natural gas before burning).
Remove SO₂ from flue gases by scrubbing with lime or limestone: CaCO₃ + SO₂ → CaSO₃ + CO₂; 2CaSO₃ + O₂ → 2CaSO₄ (gypsum).
Burn less coal and oil — use natural gas, hydro, solar and wind energy; improve efficiency; recover sulphur in industries (e.g. as H₂SO₄).
Prevention: it is better to prevent waste than to treat or clean it up afterwards.
Atom economy: design syntheses so that as many atoms of the reactants as possible end up in the product.
Less hazardous chemical syntheses and safer solvents: use and produce substances of little or no toxicity; use water or other safe solvents.
Use catalysts, renewable raw materials and energy-efficient (room temperature and pressure) processes; design products that degrade harmlessly after use.
Carbon dioxide (CO₂), methane (CH₄), nitrous oxide (N₂O) and chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs).
(Water vapour and tropospheric ozone are also greenhouse gases.)

Molecule for molecule, CFCs have a far higher global-warming potential (thousands of times that of CO₂): they absorb infrared radiation strongly in the 'atmospheric window' (8–12 μm) where other gases do not absorb, and they persist for many decades.
However, CO₂ is present in a vastly greater amount, so overall it makes the larger contribution to global warming.
Pure rain dissolves atmospheric carbon dioxide, forming the weak acid carbonic acid: CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO₃ ⇌ H⁺ + HCO₃⁻, which gives a pH of about 5.6.
When SO₂ and NOₓ from burning fuels dissolve and form strong acids (H₂SO₄, H₂SO₃, HNO₃), the pH falls below 5.6 and the rain is called acid rain.
A three-way catalytic converter (Pt, Pd and Rh on a ceramic honeycomb) removes three pollutants from vehicle exhaust at once:
carbon monoxide → CO₂ (2CO + O₂ → 2CO₂); unburnt hydrocarbons → CO₂ + H₂O; nitrogen oxides → N₂ (2NO + 2CO → N₂ + 2CO₂).
longQuestions: (i) Green chemistry is the design of chemical products and processes that reduce or eliminate the use and production of hazardous substances. Instead of treating pollution after it is made, it prevents pollution at its source — hence it is a new route to environmental protection.

Its twelve principles include: prevention of waste, atom economy, less hazardous syntheses, designing safer chemicals, safer solvents and auxiliaries (water, supercritical CO₂), energy efficiency, renewable feedstocks, reducing unnecessary steps, catalysis, design for degradation, real-time monitoring and inherently safer chemistry. Examples: the greener synthesis of ibuprofen with higher atom economy, water-based paints, biodegradable plastics, enzyme catalysts, and CO₂ instead of CFCs as blowing agents.

(ii) Greenhouse effect: short-wave radiation from the Sun passes through the atmosphere and warms the Earth's surface, which then emits long-wave infrared radiation. Greenhouse gases (CO₂, CH₄, N₂O, H₂O, CFCs) absorb this infrared and re-radiate much of it back to the surface, keeping the Earth warm (average ≈ 15 °C instead of about −18 °C) — like the glass of a greenhouse.

Global warming: burning fossil fuels, deforestation, agriculture and industry are increasing these gases, enhancing the greenhouse effect and raising the average global temperature. Consequences: melting glaciers and polar ice, rising sea levels and coastal flooding, more extreme weather (heatwaves, droughts, floods), changes in rainfall and crop yields, and loss of biodiversity.

(i) The atmosphere is the layer of gases surrounding the Earth, held by gravity: about 78% N₂, 21% O₂, 0.9% Ar, 0.04% CO₂, plus water vapour and traces of other gases. It supplies oxygen, protects from UV and meteors, and regulates temperature.

Layers (by temperature change): Troposphere (0–11/12 km) — temperature falls from about 15 °C to −56 °C; contains most of the air and water vapour; weather occurs here. Stratosphere (12–50 km) — temperature rises from −56 °C to about −2 °C because the ozone layer absorbs UV. Mesosphere (50–85 km) — temperature falls to about −92 °C, the coldest layer; meteors burn up here. Thermosphere (85–500 km) — temperature rises to about 1200 °C as gases absorb high-energy radiation; contains the ionosphere and aurorae. Exosphere — the outermost layer, merging with space.

(ii) Air pollution is the presence in the air of substances (gases, particles) in amounts that are harmful to living things or materials. Main pollutants: CO, SO₂, NOₓ, hydrocarbons, particulate matter, O₃, lead and smoke — from vehicles, industry, power plants, burning of wastes and fuels.

Effects: respiratory diseases (asthma, bronchitis, lung cancer); CO poisoning (it forms carboxyhaemoglobin and reduces oxygen transport); eye and throat irritation; acid rain; smog; depletion of the ozone layer; global warming; damage to crops, forests, buildings and metals; and reduced visibility.

(i) The ozone layer (in the stratosphere, about 15–35 km up) absorbs most of the Sun's harmful ultraviolet radiation (UV-B and UV-C, 200–315 nm). O₃ absorbs UV and splits: O₃ + hν → O₂ + O; the atoms re-form ozone: O + O₂ → O₃. In this cycle UV energy is converted into heat, warming the stratosphere and shielding life on Earth.

(ii) Without the ozone layer, intense UV radiation would reach the surface. It would cause sunburn, skin cancer and cataracts (eye damage); weaken the immune system; damage DNA and cause mutations; harm plants and reduce crop yields; kill phytoplankton, disturbing marine food chains; and degrade plastics, paints and other materials. Life on land as we know it could not survive.
Water pollution is any physical, chemical or biological change in the quality of water (rivers, lakes, seas, groundwater) that makes it harmful to humans, animals and plants or unfit for use.
Domestic sewage: organic matter, disease-causing micro-organisms (cholera, typhoid), detergents and phosphates — raising BOD and lowering dissolved oxygen.
Industrial effluents: heavy metals (Pb, Hg, Cd, Cr), acids, alkalis, dyes, oils, cyanides and other toxic chemicals from tanneries, textile mills, refineries and factories.
Agricultural run-off: fertilisers (nitrates, phosphates) causing eutrophication (algal blooms and oxygen depletion) and pesticides that accumulate in food chains.

Other sources: oil spills from tankers and pipelines; thermal pollution (hot water from power plants lowers DO); solid waste and plastics; radioactive wastes; mining and soil erosion (silt). Sources may be point (pipes, outlets) or non-point (run-off).

(a) Acid rain: SO₂ and NOₓ from burning coal, oil and vehicle fuel are oxidised in the air and dissolve in rain: 2SO₂ + O₂ → 2SO₃; SO₃ + H₂O → H₂SO₄; 4NO₂ + O₂ + 2H₂O → 4HNO₃. Rain with pH below 5.6 corrodes buildings, statues and metals; acidifies lakes and kills fish; leaches nutrients and toxic aluminium from soil, damaging forests and crops; and harms human health. Control: low-sulphur fuels, flue-gas desulphurisation, catalytic converters, cleaner energy.

(b) Smog: Classical (London) smog forms in cold, damp weather from smoke, soot, SO₂ and fog; it is reducing and causes bronchitis and breathing problems. Photochemical (Los Angeles) smog forms in warm, sunny weather from NOₓ and hydrocarbons from vehicle exhaust: NO₂ + hν → NO + O; O + O₂ → O₃; O₃ and hydrocarbons give PAN and aldehydes. It is oxidising, appears as a brown haze, irritates eyes and lungs, and damages plants and rubber.

(c) Water treatment (drinking water): screening to remove large objects; sedimentation; coagulation/flocculation with alum to settle fine particles; filtration through sand and gravel beds; disinfection by chlorination (or ozone/UV) to kill germs; sometimes softening and fluoridation. Sewage treatment: primary (physical settling), secondary (biological — activated sludge or trickling filters decompose organic matter), tertiary (chemical removal of nitrates, phosphates and remaining pollutants).

(d) Chemistry of the stratosphere: ozone is formed when UV (λ < 242 nm) splits oxygen: O₂ → 2O; O + O₂ + M → O₃ + M. It is decomposed by UV: O₃ → O₂ + O, and O + O₃ → 2O₂ (Chapman cycle), keeping a steady concentration. CFCs disturb this balance: CF₂Cl₂ + hν → CF₂Cl• + Cl•; Cl• + O₃ → ClO• + O₂; ClO• + O → Cl• + O₂ — the chlorine atom is regenerated, so one atom destroys thousands of ozone molecules. NO from high-flying aircraft acts similarly, and polar stratospheric clouds over Antarctica speed up these reactions, producing the 'ozone hole'.
activities: The cotton plug holds the sand in place, and the layer of sand acts as a filter: the spaces between the sand grains are smaller than the suspended mud and clay particles, so these particles are trapped while water passes through.
The filtered water collected in the lower part looks clear and transparent.

Note: this removes only suspended (insoluble) impurities. Dissolved salts and germs (bacteria, viruses) pass through, so the water is not yet safe to drink — it must be boiled or chlorinated. Adding layers of gravel and activated charcoal improves the filter (charcoal also adsorbs some colour and odour).
